title: Delhi Master Plan 2047: DDA sets 20-meeting target to fast-track implementation on L-G’s directions - The Tribune
content:
The Delhi Development Authority (DDA) has launched an extensive stakeholder consultation exercise to ensure the effective implementation of the Delhi Master Plan 2047, with Lieutenant-Governor (L-G) Taranjit Singh Sandhu directing the agency to engage elected representatives, government departments and key civic agencies. The DDA plans to hold around 20 meetings over three months to explain the provisions of Master Plan Delhi 2047 (MPD 2047), identify implementation challenges and strengthen coordination among agencies responsible for delivering the plan on the ground. The first consultation was held with Members of Parliament and Delhi Assembly members. The second brought together representatives of major civic, infrastructure and service agencies, including the New Delhi Municipal Council (NDMC), Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD), Delhi Jal Board (DJB), Delhi Metro Rail Corporation (DMRC), Delhi Transport Corporation (DTC), National Highways Authority of India (NHAI), National Capital Region Transport Corporation (NCRTC), Delhi Police and Delhi Urban Shelter Improvement Board (DUSIB). Representatives of several Delhi Government departments also attended, including the Public Works Department (PWD), Power Department, Land and Building Department, Fire Services, Irrigation and Flood Control Department and Forest Department. Officials and representatives from Indraprastha Gas Limited (IGL), National Buildings Construction Corporation (NBCC), Central Public Works Department (CPWD) and the Institute of Town Planners, India (ITPI) also participated in the consultations. A third stakeholder meeting focused on heritage and conservation issues. It brought together conservation bodies, architects working in heritage preservation, Delhi Tourism, the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI), School of Planning and Architecture (SPA), INTACH, the Archaeology Department, Indraprastha Heritage Redevelopment Corporation (IVPN), MCD, Delhi Urban Arts Commission (DUAC), Delhi Fire Service and the Union Ministry of Culture. During the meetings, the DDA outlined key provisions of the MPD 2047 and discussed practical aspects of its implementation, including inter-departmental coordination. Stakeholders were invited to share suggestions and flag issues that could affect the execution of the ambitious plan. The wider consultation exercise will cover a broad range of subjects under the MPD 2047, including land pooling, redevelopment of group housing, low-density areas, the Yamuna and blue-green zones, heritage conservation, mixed-use and commercial areas, in-situ slum redevelopment, decongestion and the development of education and healthcare centres. The DDA said the three-month exercise will involve a wide cross-section of stakeholders, including government agencies and service providers, industry bodies, architects and planners, resident and group-housing representatives, farmers and landowners, market and trade associations, conservation organisations, transport agencies, and representatives from the education and healthcare sectors. The consultations are intended to move the MPD 2047 beyond policy provisions and towards coordinated implementation, with the DDA seeking inputs from agencies that will ultimately be responsible for translating the plan into projects and changes on the ground. title: The BMW Adventure Bike That Quietly Does Everything Well - Top Speed
content: Subscribe to the TopSpeed newsletter to never miss an update The past few years have brought a proper overhaul to BMW’s bread-and-butter GS lineup. Not only did the flagships get an overhaul (switching from the 1250 to 1300 platform), but we also got a new entry-level F 450 GS, replacing the largely unsuccessful G 310 GS recently. As a result, the Bavarian brand’s ADV lineup is quite vast today. As much as we dig the choice, the inevitable side effect is that some bikes get less attention. BMW’s cheapest middleweight ADV is a prime example of this. It quietly does everything well, but fails to grab headlines or eyeballs due to its simple nature. Not long ago, the GS lineup started with the G 310 GS, flowed into the F 750, F 800, and F 850 GS. Then came the flagships: the R 1250 GS and R 1250 GS Adventure. Today, though, the cubic capacities have risen across the board to meet new emission norms, resulting in a larger overall lineup capacity-wise that now starts from 450 cc rather than 313 cc. The F 450 GS is the new entry into BMW’s ADV world, powered by a new parallel-twin engine. This has made all the right headlines in recent times, and global reviews only back up the impressive package. At the opposite end is the flagship R 1300 GS duo. These have a new 1,300cc boxer powerhouse and remain the most popular ADVs by the brand. That’s backed up by the sales numbers (they sell the most in the entire BMW lineup). Between these two is the middleweight trio, all of which have the 895cc parallel-twin engine. In this space, it’s the F 900 GS and F 900 GS Adventure that make all the headlines. This is down to their increased rugged appeal and near-class-leading performance. That takes the attention away from their do-it-all sibling, however, which is arguably a more logical F GS for most of us. We’re talking about the F 800 GS. It’s arguably the most vanilla GS in the lineup today, serving as the ‘jack of all trades, master of none’. So you don’t get spoke wheels (even as an option), exotic colorways, or serious off-road prowess. This is why most GS fans don’t consider it in the beginning. But look deeper, and you realize that a 19-inch front wheel for occasional off-road stints, a torque-loaded parallel-twin engine, and likable features are all packaged as standard. That means the 800 GS will happily do commuting, touring, hitting the canyons, or exploring mild trails. Its do-it-all tendencies are convincing enough, but the F 800 GS makes its case stronger via a competitive MSRP. It starts at $10,995 for the Light White colorway, with the Triple Black and Style Sport costing $295 more, respectively. That makes the 800 a sizable $3,400 cheaper than the F 900 GS. It also helps this slot well among less powerful and loaded rivals like the Suzuki V-Strom 800 and Yamaha Tenere 700. Speaking of loaded, the F 800 GS has a likable base package for the price. Let’s dive into it. The engine is arguably the highlight here. This is BMW’s popular parallel-twin powerhouse (with the 270-degree crank) we see on multiple bikes like the F 900 XR, F 900 R, and the F 900 GS duo. Here, the mill is in its most usable tune, producing 87 horsepower and 67 pound-feet. Both numbers peak at just 6,750 RPM, meaning you’ll have ample kick at all times. This also helps promise a fuel efficiency of 55 miles per gallon–a couple more than the 105-HP F 900 GS. You also get a larger four-gallon fuel tank than the F 900 GS’ 3.8-gallon unit, meaning more overall riding range. All the power reaches the wheel via a six-speed transmission, driven by a chain. The two F 900 GS models serve as the extreme kids in the lineup, featuring a 21-inch front wheel and long-travel suspension. But the F 800 GS takes a more neutral approach, just like the do-it-all R 1300 GS. So you get a 19/17-inch alloy wheel combination, paired with a bridge-type steel chassis and a simple suspension setup. The latter comprises telescopic forks and a monoshock, both with 6.7 inches of travel. Only rebound and preload are adjustable at the rear, which is a slight bummer. Twin 305 mm front discs with two-piston Brembo calipers and a rear 265 mm disc with a single-piston caliper make up the brakes. The overall neutral approach also makes the F 800 GS friendlier for the masses dimensionally. The saddle height is low at 32.1 inches, while the wheelbase is tight at 61.3 inches—both measuring less than the F 900 GS. However, its curb weight is 500 pounds, probably due to the extra fuel capacity. This is still in the ballpark of its rivals like the V-Strom 800. Although this is the cheapest midweight GS, the feature list is comparable to its F 900 siblings. A 6.5-inch TFT is front and center, armed with BMW Motorrad Connectivity. It also serves as the gateway to the rider aids, comprising cornering ABS (or ABS Pro as BMW calls it), dynamic traction control, and two ride modes. Topping this is a likable set of creature comforts like heated grips, cruise control, USB ports, adjustable levers, and all-LED lights. BMW mentions these as 'standard' inclusions in 2026, although these were previously part of the options list. If you choose the Triple Black and Style Sport colorways, you also get a taller, adjustable windscreen. Lastly, we also want to give a shoutout to the design. Unlike the distinct-looking 900 GS, the 800 GS still has the likable OG GS elements. The geometrical headlight shape is one, while the angular side fairings and front beak are other notable bits. These remind us of the ultra-popular R 1250 GS. As mentioned earlier, there are some things the F 800 GS does better than the F 900 GS, and in some aspects, it’s the other way around. So, which of the middleweight GS models is right for your riding style? If you’re on a budget and want to experience a middleweight GS with an easy-to-ride, underrated parallel-twin engine on the market today, the F 800 GS is for you. At $10,995, it is $3,400 cheaper than the F 900 GS. The next decision is how much dirt you are planning to tackle. If most of your rides are on-road with an occasional dirt road along the way, then the F 800 GS is for you. It is an adventure tourer that will feel more comfortable on the road. Another point is that the F 800 GS is the more approachable of the two motorcycles, given that it produces almost 20 ponies less than the F 900 GS. However, its weight will negate some of that approachability for newer riders to the segment. On the other hand, the F 900 GS absolutely stands out as an enduro adventurer. It’s a high-performance, lightweight ADV that can handle serious off-roading. It’s also equipped with fully adjustable top-shelf suspension, so you can dial it in as per the occasion. While more expensive, the F 900 GS is ideal if you want a middleweight Beemer that can handle everything from on-road duties to serious off-roading. We can’t ignore the F 900 GS Adventure, sitting at the very top. While built on the F 900 GS, the Adventure variant is a heavy-duty mile-muncher. It features the same 105-horsepower power output and is around 60 pounds heavier than the F 900 GS, but it makes up for it with its massive 6-gallon fuel tank, better wind protection, and optional Dynamic ESA electronic suspension. Get this if you plan to ride the breadth of the continent with some off-roading along the way. We want to hear from you. title: Dark Knight Boxer: Kevils Speed Shop’s BMW R nineT Urban G/S - Bike EXIF
content: Operating out of Paignton, Devon, along the coastal stretch of southwest England affectionately known as the English Riviera, Kevils Speed Shop has been a fixture of the custom scene since founder Kevin Hill opened its doors in 2010. Having cut its teeth on classic BMW airheads with well over 100 builds under its belt, the workshop gained international renown for building bikes for high-profile clients, including preparing Charley Boorman’s BMW R75/5 for an Arctic journey alongside Ewan McGregor. These days, Kevils operates on an unusual dual model known as Kevil's Kitchen & Speedshop: part custom motorcycle workshop, part street-food eatery serving burgers alongside retro biker culture. "It makes for an unusual combination, but motorcycles and burgers seem to work rather well together," jokes owner Kevin Hill. As the custom landscape evolved, Kevin shifted his focus from classic airheads toward modern machinery, particularly BMW’s modular R nineT platform. After BMW Motorrad UK invited Kevils to customize an R nineT for its stand at Birmingham’s NEC Motorcycle Live in 2014, the shop went on to build roughly 20 custom R nineTs. That rich pedigree brought a client from the north of England to Devon with a pristine, low-mileage 2019 BMW R nineT Urban G/S and a simple, evocative brief: build a motorcycle inspired by Batman. Movie and comic book themed custom motorcycles are notoriously difficult to execute. Too often, pop-culture builds devolve into tacky novelty props, heavy on plastic, fragile bodywork, and gimmicks that age poorly and ruin real-world rideability. Rather than relying on cartoonish graphics or bat logos, Kevin interpreted the prompt through stance, texture, and menace. "I wanted to create a motorcycle that was perfectly at home on the streets of Gotham City," Hill explains. The goal was to preserve the Urban G/S’s everyday usability while retaining the grunt of its 1,170 cc air/oil-cooled boxer twin and giving it a brooding, anti-hero aesthetic. Think Christian Bale’s Dark Knight rather than Adam West. For the first step in giving the motorcycle its atheistic , Kev installed a proprietary solo-seat conversion. Stripping away the factory rear bodywork radically shortened the bike’s visual footprint, shedding bulk while exposing the rear frame and the Öhlins rear shock. The handmade solo seat was upholstered in diamond-stitched grey leather, creating a slim, floating line that contrasts with the stock fuel tank. A tiny LED tail light was integrated beneath the seat base to keep the rear end clutter-free. Up front, the factory suspension remains internally stock, but custom fork guards were fitted to give the front end a wider, more muscular silhouette. Clamped between the triple trees sits a compact LED headlight housed within a custom, Bat-inspired nacelle equipped with a protective mesh grille, accompanied by a small auxiliary spot lamp. To back up the aggressive styling, Kevin discarded the stock airbox in favor of a pair of DNA pod filters. To ensure clean power delivery across the rev range, fueling was remapped using a Rapid Bike Evo module. Exhaust gases now exit via a pair of custom, straight-through pipes, one running down each side of the swingarm, allowing the boxer motor to bark freely. Unsurprisingly, almost every surface was refinished in black. By mixing matte, satin, and gloss finishes across the engine, frame, and bodywork, Kevin ensured the monochromatic theme retained depth rather than looking flat or washed out. The build was completed in roughly six weeks, achieved in focused evening stints after Kevin finished long days flipping burgers in the shop’s food truck. The result is a refined, perfectly proportioned daily rider. "It fulfilled the original Batman brief without becoming theatrical, and it retained the reliability and usability expected of a modern BMW," says Hill. Executing a character-inspired build without falling into tacky pop-culture tropes is a challenge, but Kevils Speed Shop nailed the brief with restraint. By prioritizing rideability, clean proportions, and subtle monochromatic textures, Kevin Hill turned a modern boxer twin into a brooding, street-legal weapon. title: Skatta Burrell Hits #1 on Billboard Global 200 as Karol G's 'BbY WOW' Samples 'Coolie Dance Riddim' - DancehallMag
content: A 23-year-old riddim just topped the Billboard Global 200. That is the story behind Karol G’s “BbY WOW,” which samples Skatta Burrell’s “Coolie Dance Riddim” and has now carried the Jamaican producer to the very top of one of music’s most competitive global charts. Karol G made the track alongside Judeline and rusowski, and the combination landed hard. BbY WOW” has crossed 100 million streams on Spotify and is currently sitting at number 16 on the Billboard Hot 100, meaning this is not just a viral moment but a sustained chart run. For Skatta Burrell, this is a full-circle moment that few producers get to experience. The “Coolie Dance Riddim” originally dropped in the early 2000s, and the fact that it is now fueling a global hit in 2025 says a lot about the staying power of classic dancehall production. There is a broader conversation happening here too. Every time a Latin or pop artist reaches back into the dancehall catalog and scores a massive hit, it reopens the debate about credit, compensation, and how the genre’s originators are recognized when their work travels this far. Skatta Burrell has been vocal in celebrating the achievement, and the dancehall community has largely rallied around the news with genuine pride. Seeing a riddim from Kingston’s golden era land at the top of a chart that spans every genre and every market is not something that happens every cycle. What makes this particularly interesting is the generational bridge it creates. Younger listeners discovering “BbY WOW” through Karol G’s fanbase are now getting pulled toward the original riddim, which is exactly the kind of organic discovery that keeps classic sounds alive rather than just sampled and forgotten. Karol G has built a reputation for pulling from unexpected sonic spaces, and this choice reflects a real ear for what makes a groove feel both fresh and rooted. The “Coolie Dance Riddim” has that low-end bounce that translates across languages and scenes, which is probably why it worked so well underneath a Spanish-language pop record in 2025. title: City unveils GS safe pet product certification - Taipei Times
content:
The New Taipei City Government on Tuesday unveiled a GS safety certificate system for pet products in collaboration with private enterprises in the industry. Incidents involving animal harm by unsafe pet products prompted the city’s Animal Protection and Health Inspection Office to develop a safety labeling system based on policies that foreign countries successfully implemented, office Deputy Commissioner Liu Hsu-fen (劉淑芬) told a news conference. Pet products using substandard materials or of poor construction pose a danger to pets, Liu said. Photo courtesy of the New Taipei City Animal Protection and Health Inspection Office A trolleys’ weight-bearing capacity, small components or sharp edges on toys and escape-proof fences are some of the design features that the GS standard evaluates before certifying a product, she said. Establishing safety standards and inspection protocols helps manufacturers to design better products and identify potential flaws to prevent harm, said Huang Hsien-ping (黃獻平), chairman of the Taipei-based China Pet Products Development Association. The GS standard obliges manufacturers to report unsafe products to the association for recall and comply with measures should a major safety incident occur, Huang said. Office Director Yang Shu-fang (楊淑方) said pet owners should think carefully about their pet’s size, physical condition, age and habits before buying products. Protecting the welfare of pets requires a regulatory system that provides comprehensive oversight from design to safety evaluation before products are released to the consumer market, an office spokesperson said. New Taipei City Government officials and association representatives at the news conference demonstrated how to check the suitability of a product for pets. title: Mr. G’s scoops up gold in Gettysburg Connection’s summer ice cream contest - Gettysburg Connection
content:
The votes are in, and the results are as sweet as expected: Mr. G’s has won the gold medal in Gettysburg Connection’s summer ice cream contest, with Half Pint Creamery’s Gettysburg location earning silver and Kilwins in Gettysburg taking bronze. Readers cast hundreds of votes on our local business listing pages to recognize their favorite places to cool off with a frozen treat. Gold medalist Mr. G’s, at 404 Baltimore St., serves homemade ice cream, soft serve, milkshakes and sundaes at the historic Twin Sycamores house. Owners Marc and Megan McLean continue a business tradition that began in 1997. The shop has occupied its current location since 2011, offering customers a place to enjoy their ice cream beneath the branches of a sycamore witness tree. Silver medalist Half Pint Creamery offers homemade, hand-dipped ice cream, with a rotating selection of flavors alongside classic favorites. Its Gettysburg shop has recently moved to 1153 Biglerville Road, where customers will find indoor and outdoor seating and parking. The creamery also offers ice cream cakes, sandwiches and cupcakes. Bronze medalist Kilwins, at 37 Steinwehr Ave., pairs its Original Recipe Ice Cream with an assortment of sweets. title: Why Global Bond Yields Are Expected to Stay Elevated - Goldman Sachs
content: We harness every resource, insight, relationship, and competitive advantage to drive superior results for our clients. Goldman Sachs’ weekly newsletter, offering economic and markets analysis from across the firm. Subscribe now. We invest the power of Goldman Sachs' financial and intellectual capital to advance enduring economic growth and opportunity. From the US to Japan and Germany, longer-maturity bond yields have climbed to the highest levels in decades. While some of the factors driving yields higher may dissipate, Goldman Sachs Research expects the fiscal concerns pushing up interest rates to persist. US government bonds that mature in 30 years yield about 5.2% (as of September 8), around the highest in more than two decades. Yields for similar-maturity bonds of Japan and the UK have climbed to the highest levels this century, and those of Germany haved reached the highest since 2009. “What’s really interesting about this move higher in yields is how orderly it’s been,” George Cole, head of European rates strategy in the Global Macro and Markets Research Group, said in a webinar. “The lack of a move higher in volatility makes it hard to claim that we’re fundamentally mispriced.” “If a view of fundamentals has carried us higher, you need a shift in fundamentals to bring us lower,” he added. There are several fundamental reasons interest rates have risen around the world, according to Goldman Sachs Research. Fiscal deficits have grown substantially in many developed economies since the Covid pandemic. Borrowing to fund investment in artificial intelligence (AI) has also soared, potentially amounting to around 1% of global GDP. With the surge in government and AI-related borrowing, there’s more competition for the pool of global savings available to fund it. At the same time, demand for bonds has diminished. Macroeconomic data has been better than expected across a range of geographies, Cole said. While recent inflation data has shown some signs of cooling, energy and food prices remain elevated. Some of the fundamental reasons for rising bond yields could reverse in the coming quarters. Goldman Sachs Research expects worries about increasing inflation from energy prices to decline in the next six months. Cole pointed out there will be more visibility into the return on AI investment, which could relieve some of the pressure on bond markets from AI-related borrowing. “But what won’t go away is the fiscal concerns,” Cole said. Will US Treasury buybacks reduce yields on 30-year Treasuries? As longer-maturity bond yields rise, governments have taken steps to adjust their issuance of longer-dated securities. Notably, the US Treasury said last month that it would increase its buybacks of Treasuries that mature in 10 years or more. Doing so will reduce the maturity-profile of US debt stock, and shorter-maturity issuance will be used to finance the buybacks. “It’s an effective reduction in the average maturity of issuance,” Cole said. “That in and of itself isn’t sufficient to change the yield level.” He points out that other governments, including the UK and Japan, have also sought to reduce their issuance of longer-maturity borrowing. Adjusting issuance across the spectrum of bond maturities is a natural supply response to shifting patterns of demand, Cole and William Marshall, head of US rates strategy, write in a report. “However, we see little evidence that these issuance responses can meaningfully impact the broader level of yields—even at the long end.” “It’s not a criticism to say that this isn’t going to change the macro price of yields,” Cole said in the webinar. “Those types of measures are perfectly consistent with the macro environment we’re in. At these levels of long-end yields, there just isn’t demand for that level of duration. There’s less interest in these long-end securities, so don’t issue them.” Goldman Sachs Research expects the global yield curve to remain steep—longer-maturity bond yields are predicted to stay relatively high compared to yields of shorter-maturity notes. The term premium that investors demand for the risk of holding longer-maturity assets is also forecast to remain higher, Cole and Marshall write. “Energy volatility continues to drive day-to-day yield moves and challenge the usefulness of bonds as a portfolio hedge,” they write. “We think this steepening will remain a feature of the rates environment as the inflationary and fiscal drivers of higher term premium remain persistent.” This article is being provided for educational purposes only. title: How Will Less Fed Transparency Affect Markets and the Economy? - Goldman Sachs
content: We harness every resource, insight, relationship, and competitive advantage to drive superior results for our clients. Goldman Sachs’ weekly newsletter, offering economic and markets analysis from across the firm. Subscribe now. We invest the power of Goldman Sachs' financial and intellectual capital to advance enduring economic growth and opportunity. Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh has steered the central bank into an era of less transparency. Former Fed governors Donald Kohn and Stephen Miran, as well as Goldman Sachs Chief Economist and Head of Goldman Sachs Research Jan Hatzius, discuss on the Goldman Sachs Exchanges podcast the merits of Fed communication and how it affects financial markets. The episode is based on the latest Top of Mind report. Allison Nathan: New Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh is steering the Fed into a less transparent era, with shorter post-meeting statements, less forward guidance, and a more limited role for projections. This marks a meaningful break from the transparency revolution that's defined central banking over the last quarter century. So, what might a less transparent Fed mean for markets and the economy? I'm Allison Nathan and this is Goldman Sachs Exchanges. Each month, I speak with investors, policymakers, and academics about the most pressing market-moving issues for our Top of Mind report from Goldman Sachs Research. For our latest edition, I spoke with former Fed governors Donald Kohn and Stephen Miran, as well as Jan Hatzius, Goldman Sachs' chief economist and head of Goldman Sachs Research. I started by asking Jan if the shift toward a less transparent Fed is a positive or negative development. Jan Hatzius: I do think that the transparency revolution in central banking over the last 40 years or so has been a good thing. If you provide significant information about your reaction function as a central bank, you say, "If we get this kind of data, then this is what we will want to do about it." Then financial markets can anticipate what is going to happen from a policy perspective. Your meeting is not until four weeks later or six weeks later, but you get surprising information, it gets incorporated in financial conditions. And then you basically have to decide whether to ratify that. But if markets have good information about what your reaction function is, what your objectives are, what you think the tools achieve, then you'll see faster monetary policy transmission in a way that you can always not ratify. That's always an option. And I think that's a great framework. And I think it's worked extremely well over the last several decades. So, I think unwinding transparency about the reaction function, in my opinion, would be bad. There's a separate question about forward guidance about the path of the policy rate. And I think there the answer is more nuanced. Economists sometimes refer to so-called Odyssean forward guidance. Odysseus tied himself to the mast. And you basically commit yourself. You say, "Here's what we're going to want to do even if the data at some point down the road tell us that maybe we should do something else." That doesn't make any sense under normal circumstances. It can make sense when you have the effective lower bound for short-term interest rates. But even then, it's a debate. Then there's so-called Delphic forward guidance. The Oracle of Delphi, the policy output is conditional on the economic data that comes in. That's more defensible, I think, even in normal times. The counter argument is market participants are going to think that what is actually supposed to be Delphic is Odyssean. But I actually like the way the Fed does this with the dot plot. The dot plot is not, in my opinion, strong forward guidance, not even strong Delphic forward guidance. It's just the views of the different FOMC participants that are implied by their economic expectations. And I do think most sophisticated observers understand the conditional nature of the dots. And they view it mostly as information about where you would be if the economy evolves in the way that the Fed expects, which is also incorporated in the summary of economic projections. And they understand that if you get a move away from that, that the policy would also change. So, I view this more as additional information about the reaction function. Allison Nathan: Don Kohn agrees that it's important for the Fed to provide clarity on its reaction function. But he sympathizes with some of Warsh's views about forward guidance and the dot plot. Donald Kohn: One thing that I've pointed to over a number of years now is the focus on the median forecast in the SEP, the economic projections of the FOMC participants. That is a very weak indication of where the committee is when just one person shifting can shift that median. And I've seen that happen every once in a while. One or two people shifting and then the market reacts. So, it's crazy to focus on that median. I think more serious is the forward guidance issue. So, here I have a little sympathy with Chairman Warsh. His concern is the forward guidance. What are we going to do next is both constraining the committee and constraining the market reaction to incoming information. And I think a good example where it constrained the committee with adverse consequences was coming out of COVID. So, the forward guidance was we're going to hold rates at zero until we're at full employment almost no matter what the inflation rate is. And I think just looking at the structure of that forward guidance, in what world is it okay to have at the highest a real rate of minus 2% at full employment? So, I think that forward guidance was not well-conceived. And I think it did constrain the committee, which is not to say that some guidance isn't helpful and at the zero lower bound may be necessary. When you get away from the zero lower bound, I think there's less need for guidance. And you can always adjust policy. So, I think forward guidance becomes much less helpful when you get away from the zero lower bound. And I would be a reluctant user. Having said that, I think the problem right now with Chairman Warsh not giving forward guidance, that's fine. Shouldn't be a problem in these circumstances. But he refuses to talk about how the committee sees the economy evolving. And I think that’s not helpful. I think explaining how the committee is thinking about the economy, what it's worried about, is part of helping the markets be stabilizing rather than destabilizing. And it's part of accountability. He's got a communications task force. I hope that one of the messages they give him is you need a narrative. You need a story. You need to be able to say what's going on, in part, because if you're not saying what's going on, how do you know when things aren't happening the way you thought they were going to happen? So, you're holding yourself accountable. Alan Greenspan, whom Chairman Warsh says he wants to imitate in many respects, always had a story. And then when things weren't evolving the way he and the committee thought they would evolve, he could see the data weren't lining up and questioned, so, what's wrong? What's going on here? So, I think the story, the narrative is really, really important. Allison Nathan: But Steve Miran is more supportive of Warsh's push for a less transparent Fed. So, Steve, do you view less transparency as a positive or a negative development? Stephen Miran: I view it as a positive development. In my view, forward guidance has dampened volatility in the short run, but the flip side of that is that it has increased it in the long run. By telling the market exactly what the Fed is going to be doing over the next several meetings or several quarters, the Fed reduced the sensitivity of financial markets to data that was coming in, because the data wouldn't really matter that much, because the Fed told you what they were going to do. But at the same time, it resulted in two elements of greater volatility over the long run. One is that it increases the likelihood that the Fed would be behind the curve, because it makes it too slow to adapt to changing conditions. And so, one thing that you saw at the end of the post-COVID experience was that the Fed was still buying mortgages when home prices were up 20%. Why was the Fed buying mortgages when home prices were up 20%? I don't think there's a really good economic reason for doing so. I think a lot of it has to do with the fact that they said they would. They gave calendar-based guidance for their activities. And that resulted in them injecting credit into the housing sector very long after it was appropriate to do so. And the result of that inflation in the housing sector, I think, was pretty plain. So, that was a very clear mistake that in my mind was a result of forward guidance. Another element of that is that I think it makes the market less good at pricing risks because the market will listen to the Fed as an indication of what's going to occur. And so, if you take a look at Silicon Valley Bank, in my mind, there's no question about it that they were terrible risk managers. Part of the reason they were terrible risk managers is because they listened to the Fed. The Fed said rates are going to be zero pretty much indefinitely. And therefore, we can extend duration in our portfolios and take much more interest rate risk. When the government tells you something is going to happen, a lot of people tend to believe that. So, I think that forward guidance, really, although it appears to dampen volatility in the short run by making the market less sensitive to any given data release, I think in the long run, you really manifest these really bad outcomes more frequently directly as a result. Allison Nathan: But Steve, isn't there an important distinction between forward guidance in the sense of committing to a predetermined policy path as you just spoke about, and the Fed being transparent about its reaction function? Stephen Miran: So, in theory, there's a very big difference. In practice, I think the difference gets a little bit muddy because the data very often require interpretation. For example, I can tell you the price of a barrel of oil because that exists. It's concrete. But inflation is the change to the general price level. The general price level doesn't exist. It gets constructed by statisticians. And in constructing the general price level, there are 10,000 methodological choices that get made along the way. And to many of these questions, there's no objectively correct answer. So, the truth is that the meaning of the inflation data changed a lot as a result of the way that these things get constructed. And sometimes they're the type of thing that monetary policy should respond to because they'd be persistent inflation that's a result of a supply/demand imbalance that monetary policy can address. And sometimes they're not the type of thing that monetary policy should respond to, either because they're a one-off, that you don't expect to be repeated. Or because they're a measurement error that you should just ignore. So, if you give too much transparency in the reaction function, then you run into situations in which you get a curveball from the data. And then you appear to be violating your reaction function or moving the goalposts. But look, I think you're right that there is a distinction between forward guidance in terms of telling people what you're going to do, and forward guidance in terms of telling people what you care about. I think that is an important distinction. And I do feel more strongly about the first than the second. So, for example, when you think about the dots, do I think the dots need reform? Absolutely. My view is the policy dot absolutely needs to go. Because as I said before, I think forward guidance increases the likelihood of large risk events. I think the policy dot contributes to that. Markets and private sector agents should not be taking the Fed's indication of where policy is going when creating their own expectations for the future. The economic dots don't have as many downsides as the policy dots. So, my view is the policy dot needs to go. But the other dots, I think that they're okay. But I think in general, you can narrow the presentation of guidance without necessarily getting rid of it altogether. Allison Nathan: Warsh has also argued that less transparency would allow markets to provide the Fed with more, quote, "direct and unfiltered," end quote, information about the economy. I asked Jan whether he agrees. Jan Hatzius: I disagree with that because markets price what they think the Fed will do, not what they think the Fed should do. And that's not going to change. If you obscure the Fed's reaction function, you're just going to have worse guesses on what the Fed will do, which would probably mean more volatility in rates markets and arguably broader financial conditions. And importantly, volatility that serves no good economic purpose. That's a really important distinction. Volatility per se isn't bad. If the outlook changes, then you would expect volatility. You get massively stronger data. Yeah, of course, that should be a hawkish shock. But if you just have less clarity about the reaction function, then market pricing is going to jump around more for not necessarily very good reasons. It also could mean that the moves that do occur just occur later. So, it takes a longer time before monetary policy is transmitted effectively to the real economy. Allison Nathan: Don, for his part, sees a middle ground. Donald Kohn: I do think the Fed being very specific about what it's going to do could damp down the market's reactions. So, if you say, "Well, I'm anticipating two interest rate decreases this year," but then the market gets some information that might suggest the rate should go up, they might not build that in. So, I think there's a golden mean here in which you give them some information. And this is perhaps what I'm thinking about with stories, narratives about what are you looking at, without saying specifically what you're going to do. And that will help the market process the new data coming in and free the market up to say, "Given what I know about the developing economic situation, given what I know about what you guys are looking at, here's what I think the path of rates needs to be for you to get to your price stability or your maximum employment objective." Allison Nathan: Don, if we presume that the outcome of less guidance is more short-term market volatility, is that a good thing or a bad thing? I mean, in other words, is that going to improve the signal or confuse the signal coming from markets? Donald Kohn: I think it could improve the signal. So, if it is damped and we take off the damper but give markets enough information to react intelligently to whatever is happening, then a little volatility is fine. It's not awful unless you're creating a lot of uncertainty about where the economy is going, what your policy is aimed at. That's going to damp investment. And so, I think creating uncertainty for the sake of uncertainty is not a productive thing to do. That's another way of saying not telling the story is what creates volatility. So, I do think there's something to be said for backing off from the specific guidance, but you need to help the markets figure out what the right path of rates is to accomplish your objectives. Allison Nathan: And Steve Miran seems most convinced that reducing transparency would improve the market signal and says higher volatility is an unavoidable, but ultimately acceptable cost. Stephen Miran: If you're given forward guidance, there's very little volatility and there's no signal in the front end. It just reflects the forward guidance. If you're not getting forward guidance, there's volatility and there's signal. And just because there's volatility doesn't mean that there's no signal, right? Market behavior is always going to come with volatility. Markets will always be volatile. But if you hope to get any signal from markets whatsoever, you have to accept that volatility. The first best world of market signal without volatility doesn't exist. So, you can't let perfection be your standard. There is no possible world in which you can get a strong market signal without volatility. So, you've got to accept volatility along with the market signal. Allison Nathan: With so much at stake, I've then asked just how durable a less transparent Fed regime could be. Here's what Jan had to say. Jan Hatzius: I think it's an open question. The Chairman can, of course, make a lot of changes in terms of the regime. He controls what he says at the press conference, for example. That's something that nobody can take away from him. And if he wants to provide less information, then he can provide less information. So, in that sense, it could be durable. But we'll see what the consequences are. The other question is, to what extent can a reduction in trade communications broadly defined as, say, the number of speeches, how likely is that going to be durable? That is not going likely to be durable, because I think the Reserve Bank presidents, you're not going to be able to shut them down. And they have strong incentives to continue to talk because that is their main role. And the boards of directors of the regional Federal Reserve Banks have a pretty strong incentive to have their presidents talk a lot. Increasingly, as a Reserve Bank, you are what your president brings to the table in terms of the monetary policy debate. So, the cacophony could get worse if you have less centralized communication but a continued high level of talk from the Reserve Bank presidents. Allison Nathan: But Don views Warsh's current level of quietness as unsustainable. Donald Kohn: I don't think the degree of quietness just from Chairman Warsh is sustainable. And I'm guessing that he knows that the July press conference was not a good look for a Fed chair. So, you go through a press conference. Short-term rates go down and long-term rates go up. So, long-term rates are building in inflation or uncertainty premiums, risk premiums, term premiums. I'm sure that's not what he would have wanted going into the press conference. This is a very smart man. I worked very closely with him for nearly four years. Our offices were next to each other at the Fed. We worked hand-in-hand through the financial crisis. So, I'm confident that Chairman Warsh recognizes that there's a void he needs to move in the direction of filling. I'm also confident that the Communications Task Force will help move him in that direction. Allison Nathan: And while Steve believes that a sharp rise in volatility could force Warsh to rethink his strategy, he says we're far from that point today. Steve, even if Chairman Warsh wants to have a quieter Fed, we all know that at some point volatility can get quite disruptive. So, is there a threshold at which that volatility is just unsustainable? Stephen Miran: Absolutely. So, let me put it this way. A number of tools that were introduced in the GFC era, forward guidance, QE, the formal inflation target. These are extraordinary tools for use at the zero lower bound when you are afraid of deflation risk that you can't head off. In that environment, it is appropriate, in my view, to use those tools. Would I have opposed these tools in 2009/2010? No, I would not have. By the time you get to 2014/2015, are they needed anymore? Absolutely not. They all should have been repealed at that point completely. You use these tools when you need them. You take antibiotics when you're sick. If you take antibiotics when you're not sick, you just create super bugs. And that's what we saw, I think, with the example before where they didn't stop buying MBS. And so, these tools, if you have an economic environment that suits them, are useful. But they become less useful outside of that economic environment. And their preciousness shouldn't be squandered. So, if the increase in volatility is so much that it brings you back to the zero lower bound and you can offset it with a lower Fed funds rate. Then sure, forward guidance might be appropriate. But we're very, very far from that type of outcome. Allison Nathan: So, with all of this in mind, we'll be closely watching how Fed communication evolves from here. Let's leave it there for now. My thanks to Don Kohn, Steve Miran, and Jan Hatzius. And thank you for listening to this episode of Goldman Sachs Exchanges, which was recorded in August 2026. I'm Allison Nathan. title: Karol G’s “BbY WOW,” Sampling Iconic Coolie Dance Riddim, Tops Billboard Global Charts - Kaboom Magazine
content: Our latest digital magazine is available for download - CLICK HERE >> The Colombian Latin superstar’s collab with Judeline and Rusowsky dethrones Shakira and Burna Boy’s “Dai Dai” from atop the Billboard Global Excl. U.S. chart after generating 42.3 million global streams in a week and surpassing 103 million Spotify plays Colombian Latin superstar Karol G, alongside Spanish artistes Judeline and rusowsky, has climbed to No. 1 on both the Billboard Global 200 and Billboard Global Excl. U.S. charts with their collaboration, “BbY WOW.” The achievement gives Karol G her second leader on both global charts, following “TQG,” her collaboration with fellow Colombian superstar Shakira, which debuted at No. 1 in March 2023. For Judeline and rusowsky, “BbY WOW” marks their first No. 1 on either ranking. The track, which samples Jamaican producer Skatta Burrell’s iconic Coolie Dance riddim, has already surpassed 103 million streams on Spotify. According to Luminate, “BbY WOW” generated 42.3 million streams worldwide from August 28 to September 3, a 62% increase week over week, while selling 1,000 downloads globally, up 60%. The surge makes “BbY WOW” the biggest song in the world on Billboard’s global rankings, dethroning Shakira and Burna Boy’s “Dai Dai,” which previously spent 10 weeks atop Global Excl. U.S. and seven weeks at No. 1 on the Global 200. Released in 2003, Skatta Burrell’s Coolie Dance riddim has enjoyed a remarkable global reach over the past two decades, with its distinctive sound sampled and incorporated into music stretching from Latin America to India, the Arab world and the U.S. pop scene. The latest success also arrives amid renewed conversation around the influence of Jamaican production on global music. Iconic Jamaican production duo Steely & Clevie were recently dealt a major legal setback in their sweeping copyright case involving reggaeton’s signature Dem Bow riddim, after Bad Bunny and several other defendants secured a significant victory. Filed in 2021, the sprawling case has targeted nearly 2,000 songs involving more than 150 artistes, with major names including Bad Bunny, Karol G, Drake and Justin Bieber among those connected to the litigation. Under the agreement, Goldman Sachs Asset Management’s multi-asset solutions team will assume portfolio-management responsibilities for five IG Strategic Wealth Portfolios. The portfolios provide Canadian investors exposure to diversified strategies spanning equities, fixed income and alternatives. Over the past several years, Goldman has been focused on building a larger, capital-light AWM franchise and reducing its dependence on more volatile, balance-sheet-intensive revenues. wealth management, alternatives and solutions have been identified as three major growth opportunities within AWM. Management and other fees, together with private banking and lending revenues, saw a compound annual rate of 12% from 2021 through 2025, with the rising trend continuing in the first half of 2026, highlighting the increasing importance of durable revenues to Goldman’s earnings mix. Goldman has supported this strategy through partnerships and targeted acquisitions. In September 2025, it partnered with T. Rowe Price TROW to develop public-private investment solutions for wealth and retirement clients. Goldman also acquired Innovator Capital Management in April 2026, adding about $31 billion in assets under supervision and strengthening its defined-outcome ETF capabilities. In August 2026, it agreed to acquire NEOS Investments, which manages roughly $30 billion. Together, NEOS, Innovator and Goldman’s existing operations are expected to create a $130-billion global ETF platform, expanding its reach among advisors and wealth-management clients. GS entered an agreement in August 2026 to acquire LCN Capital Partners, adding a specialist investment platform focused on sale-leaseback, build-to-suit and triple-net-lease real estate investments. Collectively, these moves demonstrate Goldman’s strategy of adding differentiated investment capabilities that can attract third-party assets and generate recurring management fees. Overall, the IG Wealth Management collaboration underscores Goldman’s continued focus on scaling AWM and building a more durable revenue base. Alongside the T. Rowe Price partnership and the Innovator, NEOS and LCN transactions, the latest collaboration strengthens GS’s third-party distribution capabilities and broadens its addressable wealth-management market. Over time, successful expansion of these relationships should support recurring fee growth, improve the quality of Goldman’s revenue mix and further advance its transition toward a more capital-light business model. Two close peers of GS are JPMorgan JPM and Morgan Stanley MS, which are also making efforts to expand their AWM businesses. JPMorgan’s AWM segment is a steadier, fee-led profit engine inside the bank, spanning asset management and the private bank. title: GS Department of World Languages and Cultures professor named executive director of national French honor society, Pi Delta Phi - Grice Connect
content: In early August, French Professor Olga Amarie, Ph.D., in Georgia Southern University’s Department of World Languages and Cultures, was named the newest executive director of the board of Pi Delta Phi, the oldest national academic honor society for a world language within the United States. The organization also provides opportunities for students to connect with leading scholars in French studies and assists students in applying for study abroad scholarships. However, Amarie’s involvement extends beyond her current title. “I joined Pi Delta Phi as a graduate student at the University of Notre Dame, chapter Mu Phi. It is not common for European universities to have honor societies for each specific field. It was completely new and interesting for me as an international student,” she said. In 2012, Amarie took her commitment to the organization and the students it serves a step further. “Dr. David Seaman, emeritus, advised me to visit the Pi Delta Phi board at the Rocky Mountain Modern Language Association Conference because they had an open session, which I did,” Amarie said. “Soon after, I volunteered to serve as vice president for the society and opened nine chapters of Pi Delta Phi,” Amarie said. Although this is her first time with the Executive Director title, this veteran educator has spent more than three decades devoting her career to supporting future generations of French scholars. “The responsibilities are new but something I like to do: maintain all sorts of records for the society; represent the society at the annual meeting of the Association of College Honor Societies; work with chapter moderators on Pi Delta Phi materials; and work with scholarship recipients who will study abroad in Chicoutimi, Canada, and in Paris, Aix-en-Provence, France, etc.,” Amarie said. As technology continues to rapidly evolve, Amarie stresses the importance of world culture and language as an integral part of human connection, scholarship and meaningful advancement. “Many employers value multilingual employees. I personally speak four languages: Romanian, French, English and Russian. Foreign language skills are useful in many fields, including education, business, health care, government, tourism, international relations and technology. Being bilingual or multilingual can make job candidates more competitive,” she said. Looking ahead while honoring history, Amarie anticipates future generations of eager undergraduate and graduate students as they explore academic and career opportunities, connecting scholars from across the globe and unifying learners through their shared admiration and commitment to French language and Francophone literatures. “The motto of Pi Delta Phi is very inspirational: «Avançons, amis fidèles de la culture française», which means, ‘Let us move forward, faithful friends of French culture,’” she said. “I like this motto because it emphasizes both growth (avançons) and commitment (fidèles) to French studies. We work together toward shared language, cultural traditions and values.”

title: GS E&R, KOSPO Team Up to Convert Coal Plants to LNG - Seoul Economic Daily
content:
MOU Signed on Joint Development of New Power Generation Projects
Coal Facilities to Be Converted to LNG to Cut Carbon Emissions GS E&R is moving to phase out coal and expand low-carbon energy supply by converting aging coal-fired combined heat and power facilities in industrial complexes to liquefied natural gas, in partnership with Korea Southern Power Co. GS E&R said on the 9th that it had signed a memorandum of understanding with Korea Southern Power, or KOSPO, on joint cooperation in new power generation development projects. The signing ceremony was held the previous day and was attended by GS E&R Chief Executive Hwang Byung-so and KOSPO President Kim Jun-dong, among others. The two companies will jointly pursue the conversion of aging coal-fired combined heat and power plants into LNG-based facilities. The plan is to replace existing coal-centered generation equipment with LNG facilities that emit less carbon, producing cleaner heat and electricity while reducing carbon emissions at tenant companies to strengthen their export competitiveness. GS E&R currently supplies process heat to companies operating in national industrial complexes including Banwol, Gumi and Pocheon. The company also operates a 126-megawatt wind power complex in Yeongyang County, North Gyeongsang Province. The two sides plan to cooperate on drawing up plans for the LNG fuel conversion and modernization project, reviewing technologies for eco-friendly heat and power supply, conducting feasibility studies and handling permits and approvals. "We will build a stable and environmentally friendly foundation for energy supply so that the regional economy can continue sustainable growth," Hwang said. title: GS Caltex to Supply 2,000 Tons of Sustainable Jet Fuel to DHL Express - Seoul Economic Daily
content:
One-Year SAF Supply Deal Meets EU Renewable Energy Directive
Refiner to Build Dedicated Co-Processing Production Line GS Caltex, a unit of GS Holdings (078930.KS), is expanding its biofuel business by supplying sustainable aviation fuel to international express delivery company DHL Express. GS Caltex said on the 9th that it had signed a memorandum of understanding with DHL Express to build a partnership for carbon reduction based on sustainable aviation fuel, or SAF. Kim Chang-soo, executive vice president of GS Caltex, and John Pearson, chief executive officer of DHL Express, attended the signing ceremony along with other senior officials from both companies. Under the agreement, GS Caltex will supply SAF for one year to aircraft that DHL Express refuels in South Korea. The fuel is produced through co-processing and has received ISCC EU certification, which meets the European Union's Renewable Energy Directive. The volume totals 2,000 tons on a neat SAF basis. Co-processing is a method in which petroleum-based feedstock and bio-based feedstock from plants and animals are fed together into existing refining facilities. GS Caltex will also join DHL Express's GoGreen Plus program. GoGreen Plus is a service through which DHL Express helps customers cut carbon emissions generated during transportation by using SAF. The program will apply to all goods the refiner ships overseas through DHL Express, allowing it to receive credit for the emissions reductions. GS Caltex plans to keep expanding SAF production and supply to airlines. To that end, the company is building a dedicated co-processing production line. It involves constructing dedicated piping that connects tanks reserved for bio-based feedstock to refining processes, enabling commercial-scale SAF output. GS Caltex plans to expand SAF production through co-processing within this year. "This SAF supply to DHL Express takes us one step further in expanding our customer base," an official at GS Caltex said. "We will continue to grow our biofuel business, including SAF, in line with market demand." GS Caltex took part in a biofuel demonstration study run by the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy in 2023, receiving SAF from Finnish biofuel producer Neste. In 2024, it produced SAF by blending the fuel with conventional jet fuel and exported it to Narita Airport in Japan. title: GS Caltex to supply DHL Express with 2,000 tons of SAF - The Korea Herald

Business GS Caltex to supply DHL Express with 2,000 tons of SAF GS Caltex will supply sustainable aviation fuel to DHL Express in Korea, expanding its presence in the fast-growing market for lower-carbon aviation fuels. The two companies signed a memorandum of understanding Tuesday at GS Tower in southern Seoul to cooperate on reducing aviation and logistics emissions through SAF. Kim Chang-soo, vice president of GS Caltex’s Mobility and Marketing Division, and DHL Express CEO John Pearson attended the signing ceremony. Under the agreement, GS Caltex will supply fuel for DHL Express aircraft operating in Korea for one year. The deal covers 2,000 metric tons of neat SAF, an unblended form of the alternative fuel that can be mixed with conventional jet fuel before use. The SAF was produced through co-processing, in which renewable feedstocks are processed alongside petroleum-based materials at an existing refinery. It has received ISCC EU certification for compliance with the European Union’s Renewable Energy Directive. GS Caltex will also participate in DHL Express’ GoGreen Plus program, which uses SAF to reduce air freight emissions. The program will cover all products shipped by GS Caltex through DHL Express. To meet growing demand, GS Caltex plans to expand its production capacity by completing a dedicated co-processing line by the end of this year, enabling commercial-scale SAF output. The refiner has expanded its domestic and overseas SAF operations since 2023. As part of a biofuel demonstration project led by the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy, it supplied fuel for Korea’s first SAF test flights with Korean Air. In 2024, GS Caltex exported SAF blended with Neste’s neat SAF to Japan’s Narita Airport through trading company Itochu. The deal made it the first Korean refiner to commercially sell SAF certified under ISCC CORSIA, an international standard for aviation fuels. title: The Short Lived Performance Car That Deserved Better - HotCars
content: Jared has spent 15 years covering the auto industry, getting his first break with autoX—one of Asia’s biggest auto magazines. Since 2010, he has reviewed hundreds of cars and motorbikes around the world, worked with Top Gear, Autocar, Evo, Motoring World, and Quattroruote, served on the IMOTY jury for five years, and is a founding member of the Automotive Journalist Association of India (AJAI). Subscribe to the HotCars newsletter to never miss an update BMW M-Cars wrote the rulebook for the performance sedan. Audi has long been a formidable presence in the segment, and Mercedes perfected the "German muscle car" with their V8-powered AMGs, but credible non-German challengers have always been rare. What makes the landscape even more challenging is that the market has been shifting decisively away from traditional performance vehicles. Sports cars are few and far between, coupes that are not dedicated sports cars are nearly extinct, and SUVs and crossovers have become the default choice for most buyers. The SUV craze began in the late 1990s and early 2000s, with pioneers like the Toyota RAV4 and Honda CR-V anchoring the economy end of the spectrum, while the Mercedes-Benz ML and the Lexus RX300 effectively invented the modern luxury crossover class. We've added more insights into what makes this sedan's V8 engine special and how to extract more power from it without ruining its character. With crossovers now the industry standard, performance cars have had to evolve in tandem. You can't build a performance variant of a vehicle you no longer sell — and since automakers are moving crossovers the way McDonald's moves burgers and fries, while sedans are quietly fading like Circuit City and RadioShack, it only makes sense that the ranks of performance sedans and coupes have thinned considerably. There is nothing inherently wrong with something like the X5M, but performance sedans have always held a special appeal for enthusiasts that no SUV has quite managed to replicate. Thankfully, there are still some fantastic performance sedans on the market — but there is one in particular that deserved to stick around a little longer. The muscle car is American, the exotic sports car Italian, and the performance saloon German. Obviously, this is a generalization, but such widely held perceptions of certain market segments have a real impact on how consumers shop. A common critique levied at something like the Genesis G90 is that it isn't quite up to the standard of the S-Class. That isn't entirely untrue, but buyers often begin their evaluation of a Genesis, Acura, Cadillac, or Lexus by assuming it could never surpass a “proper” German luxury sedan. While American, Japanese, and Korean automakers have all built exceptional luxury and performance sedans, overcoming those deeply ingrained perceptions remains an uphill battle. Much like General Motors and John DeLorean inventing the muscle car in 1964, BMW ostensibly invented the modern sports sedan in 1984 with the introduction of the E28 M5. The first-ever M5 was powered by a 3.5L I6 that produced 256 horsepower in the North American market. The iconic E30 M3 arrived just two years later, and two years after that the second-generation M5, the E34, upped displacement to 3.6L (3.8L post-facelift in Europe) and pushed output past 300 horsepower. And if the E34 didn't cement the M5 legacy, the legendary 4.9L V8-powered E39 most certainly did. Mercedes followed suit in 1993 with the first production AMG, the C36. In the years that followed, some incredible cars continued the lineage — the C36 gave way to the V8-powered C43, C55, and C63. The E39 was succeeded by the 5.0L V10-powered E60, and Audi was busy fitting V8s and V10s into its S and RS cars throughout the 2000s. Just as the Mustang defined the pony car, these German sports sedans defined their segment, making it that much harder for outside competitors to carve out a lasting place. Find a car enthusiast and ask them which sports sedan on the current market would be their pick. If you ask me? I'll take a Cadillac CT5-V Blackwing, thank you very much. And it's not just because you get a 6.2L supercharged V8 producing 650 horsepower — borrowed from the C7 Z06 — paired with the brilliant MagneRide suspension. No, despite my great appreciation for many automatics, I simply prefer a manual transmission. I'm certainly not in the minority, and aside from the M3, Cadillac is the only other game in town when it comes to rowing your own gears in a four-door sedan. No manual has been offered in the M5 since the F10 generation, and no manual has appeared in an Audi sports sedan since the B8.5 S4 — or the B7 RS4 if you want the full-fat performance model. Cadillac, meanwhile, offers both the CT4-V and CT5-V Blackwing with 6-speed manuals. The CT5-V Blackwing is the spiritual heir to the original V-car, the CTS-V. When it arrived in 2004 with the 405-horsepower LS6 V8 borrowed from the C5 Corvette Z06, it was the last thing anyone expected from Cadillac. At the time, the brand was riding high on the second-generation Escalade and still selling the DeVille and Seville. There was already plenty of surprise in 2003 when the CTS 3.6L became the first Cadillac offered with a manual transmission since the 1988 Cimarron — nobody was expecting the original CTS-V on top of that, let alone a second generation that paired a manual transmission with 556 supercharged horsepower from the LSA V8. We're quite lucky the CT4-V and CT5-V Blackwing models have carried that torch, because the Pontiac GXP and Chevy SS came and went faster than the Honda Prologue. The Cadillac offerings have been among the absolute best in this segment for the better part of two decades. The CTS-V and ATS-V — and their successors, the CT4-V and CT5-V Blackwing — are arguably even better than their respective M5 and M3 counterparts, proving that American brands have a legitimate claim in this space. Japanese and Korean brands have made attempts, but have struggled to establish a long-term foothold. Aside from Lexus, Infiniti and Genesis are the only two of the bunch to have offered a V8, but the M56/Q70 5.6L and G80 5.0L fall well short of true sports sedan status. The Kia Stinger GT2, Genesis G70 3.3T, Infiniti Q50 Red Sport, and Acura TLX Type S are all fantastic cars, but they compete more directly with cars like the S4, M340i, C43 AMG, and the CT4-V (non-Blackwing) than with M Division, AMG, or Blackwing at the top. Lexus is really the only one of the bunch to have genuinely gone after BMW — first with the IS-F, and then with one of the all-time great performance sedans. The GS-F was based on the fourth-generation Lexus GS, introduced in 2011. Unlike the previous generation of GS, which offered V8 trims such as the GS 400, 430, and 460, the final iteration of the Lexus GS was V6-only. It was an excellent V6 — the 3.5L 2GR-FE/FKS — but it didn't quite pack the punch of the V8 cars. That's fine, though, because for the final generation Lexus saved the V8 for something more special: the GS-F. While the previous V8 trims were essentially engine upgrades, the GS-F was a proper sports sedan. It was Lexus's second entry into that market, following the 2008–2014 IS-F. It used the same 8-speed automatic and 5.0L V8 as the IS-F, but produced 51 more horsepower than its predecessor. And as noted, the GS-F is far more than just an engine. Starting in 2017, models received adaptive variable suspension (AVS), which allows the car to adjust the dampers independently across 30 different settings based on driver input, selected mode, and real-time sensor data. All GS-F models also received a torque-vectoring differential that can be set to standard, slalom, or track mode. This is not to be confused with brake torque vectoring, as found on a Fiesta ST — this is a proper mechanical trick diff that automotive journalists consistently praised for allowing this large sedan to rotate through corners like a much smaller machine. The GS-F was also fitted with Brembo 6-piston front and 4-piston rear brakes, giving the driver genuine confidence when scrubbing off speed. The GS-F shares the same wonderful powertrain as the IS-F and RC-F, using the same Aisin AA80E 8-speed automatic — though the GS-F has a shorter final drive ratio than the IS-F and RC-F — and the 2UR-GSE 5.0L V8. Which is to say, it works. The AA80E, which debuted in the 2007 LS 460 as the world's first production 8-speed automatic, has earned an excellent long-term reputation. It most recently appeared in the IS 500 F Sport Performance, which shares the same mechanical core as the proper F models. Both the 2UR-GSE and the Aisin 8-speed are genuinely reliable units. In fact, the entire car is, which is why these have held 60%–70% of their value since new. According to classic.com and comparable sales from major auction sites, the GS-F is currently valued at nearly double that of an equivalent M5 from the same era, despite the performance gap. It's true that contemporary rivals — the aforementioned M5, CTS-V, E63, and RS7 — all made more power and could outpace the GS-F's already brisk 4.4-second sprint to 60 mph. That was a legitimate critique when the car was new, but 467 horsepower and 389 lb-ft of torque are not small numbers. We've been desensitized to power figures that include a comma, but a 193-inch, 4,100-pound sedan reaching 60 mph in the same time as a 981 Cayman S is genuinely impressive. And besides — are you really taking this to the track? Are you racing for pinks? The GS-F may not have been the outright performance king of its era, but given its reliability and its glorious engine note, it deserved another chance. It only lasted five model years, after all. Sadly, though it's possible Toyota could one day fit the 4.0L twin-turbo V8 from the GR GT3 into a new Lexus sports sedan, the sedan market may not survive long enough for that to happen. Lexus currently only offers the front-wheel-drive ES in the sedan segment. Thankfully, the GS-F appears reliable enough to last for decades — just don't expect prices to fall; the market has already figured out how special these cars are. It's just a shame there won't be another. Fun Fact: Before the GS F reached showrooms, Lexus engineers subjected it to the Nürburgring Nordschleife, Fuji Speedway, and Autopolis, using some of the world's toughest circuits to sharpen its handling and performance. Part of the reason the GS F feels so special is hiding under its hood:     Toyota's 2UR-GSE, widely regarded as one of the automaker's finest modern naturally aspirated engines. Rather than relying on forced induction like most of its rivals, Lexus built this 5.0-liter V8 around high-rpm breathing, sharp response, and durability. The formula starts with free-breathing cylinder heads developed by Yamaha, while lightweight forged connecting rods and titanium intake and exhaust valves help the V8 spin to a 7,300-rpm redline. The D-4S fuel system combines direct and port injection, allowing the engine to run a high 12.3:1 compression ratio without sacrificing everyday drivability. VVT-iE adds another clever trick. During steady cruising, the engine can run the Atkinson cycle for better efficiency; step on the gas, and it switches to the Otto cycle for stronger performance. The GS F may have looked outgunned by German rivals on paper, but that misses the point. The 2UR-GSE was engineered for immediacy, revs, and character—not a dyno-sheet arms race. It's a big V8, but it was developed with a surprisingly sophisticated purpose. What if you want more than 467 horsepower from your GS F? The car's output was always a sore spot beside 600-horsepower     German sports sedans, and while Lexus made up ground with refinement and character, some owners will still want more. Fortunately, the 2UR-GSE has powered several Lexus performance models since the 2000s, giving it a healthy aftermarket. One upgrade is the RR Racing-tuned PPE header, which RR Racing estimates can add 25–35 whp, or 40–48 whp when paired with its tune. Freer-flowing exhaust components, intake upgrades, and ECU calibration can build on those gains. The catch is that a naturally aspirated V8 doesn't respond like a turbo engine. There is no boost pressure to turn up, so gains come from improving airflow, combustion, and calibration rather than simply increasing boost. That makes the smartest GS F builds less about chasing a giant dyno number and more about making this already special V8 breathe and respond even better. Luxury performance sedans are notorious for shedding value once they leave the showroom. The Lexus GS F hasn't escaped depreciation entirely, but it has aged far more gracefully on the used market than its German rivals. With an original MSRP ranging from about $84,440 for 2016 models to more than $90,000 for a well-optioned 2020 example, the GS F has become more attainable over time, yet it remains remarkably resistant to the steep value drops that typically define this segment. Today, early 2016–2017 cars typically trade anywhere from the high-$30,000s to around $50,000, depending on mileage and condition, while facelifted 2018–2020 examples — which received updated styling and additional standard technology — regularly command well over $50,000. Exceptional low-mileage cars can fetch considerably more, as demonstrated by a 20,000-mile 2020 GS F that sold for $73,500 on Bring a Trailer in early 2025. Meanwhile, buyers can still pick up an F10 BMW M5 for less than $30,000, and even the rare S212 Mercedes-Benz E 63 AMG often changes hands for under $40,000. The contrast highlights just how well the GS F has protected its value. Lexus' hard-earned reputation for reliability is undoubtedly part of the equation, but it's far from the only reason. Lexus' reputation for bulletproof reliability is certainly part of the reason the GS F has depreciated far less than its European rivals, but it's far from the whole story. There are other reasons, starting with sheer rarity. The collector market tends to reward cars that combine genuine performance with genuine scarcity, and the Lexus GS F checks both boxes. While BMW and Mercedes-AMG built their M5 and E63 in far greater numbers, Lexus produced roughly 4,823 GS Fs worldwide during the model's five-year run, with only about 2,347 examples reaching U.S. buyers. Special editions and uncommon specifications only amplify that exclusivity — the 2019 10th Anniversary Edition was capped at 100 U.S. cars, while rare finishes such as Flare Yellow and Molten Pearl have become especially sought-after among enthusiasts. Just as important is what's under the hood. The GS F's 5.0-liter 2UR-GSE V8 belongs to a rapidly shrinking breed of naturally aspirated performance engines, particularly in the sports sedan world. It rewards drivers with immediate throttle response, a broad and predictable power curve, a 7,300-rpm redline, and an exhaust note that no turbocharged engine can quite replicate. Those qualities are even more compelling today, given that there is no naturally aspirated V8 sports sedan currently on sale. After spending so much time praising the GS F, it's fair to ask why Lexus discontinued it after the 2020 model year. The answer has less to do with the GS F itself and more to do with the fate of the GS sedan it was built upon. By the end of its run, the GS had become financially unsustainable. Lexus sold just 3,378 GSs in the U.S. during 2019, accounting for only 4% of the brand's passenger-car sales and less than 1% of the midsize luxury sedan segment. The GS was also squeezed from both sides. Buyers seeking comfort overwhelmingly chose the less expensive ES, while those wanting practicality flocked to the RX, which routinely sold well into six figures annually. With engineering resources increasingly directed toward crossovers, the aging fourth-generation GS received only incremental updates, leaving its interior technology and overall package trailing newer European competitors. As impressive as the GS F was, it couldn't reverse those trends. Against 600-plus-horsepower twin-turbo rivals like the BMW M5 and Mercedes-AMG E 63, its 467-horsepower naturally aspirated V8 appealed to a niche audience. Combined with Lexus' smaller performance-brand footprint, the GS F simply wasn't enough to save the GS nameplate. The GS F belongs to a category that has effectively disappeared. You can no longer walk into a dealership and buy a naturally aspirated V8 sports sedan. Nearly every manufacturer has downsized to turbocharged six-cylinder engines or electrified powertrains in pursuit of stricter emissions targets and improved fuel economy. Even the remaining V8-powered performance sedans rely almost exclusively on forced induction to achieve their staggering power figures. They are undeniably quicker, but they lack the immediate throttle response, progressive power delivery, and intoxicating high-revving character that defined the GS F. To its credit, Lexus kept that philosophy alive a little longer with the IS 500 F SPORT Performance. Sharing the GS F's 5.0-liter 2UR-GSE V8, the smaller sedan produced a slightly improved 472 horsepower and wrapped it in a lighter, more agile package that many enthusiasts considered the spiritual successor to the GS F. The IS 500 F SPORT Performance demonstrated that Lexus still believed there was an audience for a naturally aspirated V8 luxury sports sedan, but it ultimately proved not large enough to overcome market realities.     Production ended after the 2025 model year, bringing Lexus' naturally aspirated V8 sedan lineage to a close. As emission regulations tighten and electrification accelerates, cars like the GS F are becoming relics of a different era. Enthusiasts continue to ask for naturally aspirated V8 sports sedans, but the industry is moving in a different direction. That only makes the GS F more desirable today — not just as a great driver's car, but as a reminder of a performance philosophy that may never return.
