                                    2026.09.09 GS Caltex (Board Chair & CEO, GS Caltex / Vice Chairman, GS Group, Saehong Hur) announced that it will supply sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) to the global logistics provider DHL Express, marking a further expansion of its SAF supply activities. The two companies signed a memorandum of understanding to establish a “partnership for carbon reduction based on sustainable aviation fuel” on September 8 at GS Tower in Gangnam, Seoul. Representatives from both companies, including Changsoo Kim, Executive Vice President of Mobility & Marketing at GS Caltex, and John Pearson, CEO of DHL Express, attended the signing ceremony. Under the agreement, GS Caltex will supply SAF to aircraft operated by DHL Express that refuel in Korea over the next year. The total volume to be supplied to DHL Express is equivalent to 2,000 tons of Neat SAF (100% SAF). The SAF to be supplied by GS Caltex to DHL Express is produced through a co-processing method and is ISCC EU certified in compliance with the European Union’s Renewable Energy Directive. In addition, GS Caltex will participate in DHL Express’s GoGreen Plus program. GoGreen Plus is a service that helps reduce carbon emissions generated during transportation through the use of SAF. Going forward, all shipments sent overseas by GS Caltex through DHL Express will use GoGreen Plus and GS Caltex will receive recognition for the resulting carbon reductions. GS Caltex plans to expand SAF production and supply to airlines as market demand grows. To support the expansion while ensuring stable supply, the company will establish a dedicated co-processing production line. The project will include dedicated pipelines connecting bio-feedstock tanks to refinery processes to enable commercial-scale SAF production. GS Caltex is set to complete the dedicated co-processing production line within the year and expand SAF production. A GS Caltex spokesperson said, “Through the SAF supply agreement with DHL Express, we have taken another step toward expanding the SAF customers,” adding, “We will continue to expand the SAF business and other areas of our biofuel business in response to market demand.” Beyond its supply to DHL Express, GS Caltex has continued to produce and supply SAF in response to developments in the global fuel market and government policies. In 2023, as part of the company’s participation in the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy’s Biofuel Demonstration Research Project, GS Caltex sourced SAF from Neste, a Finnish biofuel producer. In September of the same year, the company began Korea’s first SAF fueling and demonstration flights with Korean Air, successfully completing six flights in total. title: Mama G’s to hold fundraiser after car crash killed one employee and seriously injured another - Springfield Daily Citizen

Mama G’s Kitchen (210 S. Market Ave.) is holding a fundraiser on Sunday, Sept. 13, to benefit the families of one employee who was killed and another who was seriously injured in a crash last week on Kearney Street. Tesia Ta, 34, and Kayle Moore, 27, were on their way to dinner around 10:48 p.m. on Sept. 2. Moore made a left-hand turn, crossing into the path of another driver, 25-year-old Marquis Starks. Ta died at the hospital, while both Moore and Starks were left with life-threatening injuries. Moore is a mother of three. On Friday, Sept. 4, Mama G’s owner Gloria Hairston said she was in stable condition and able to talk. She had a close friendship with Ta, according to Hairston. Family members and people who worked with Ta described her as positive, hardworking and “the life of the party.” As a bartender, she was well-known to customers. title: The Japanese Luxury Sedan That Could Actually Challenge BMW - HotCars
content: Eric Tipan has spent more than 30 years working across journalism, broadcasting and live media. He’s a five-time Henry Ford Award winner, has covered the Olympic Games for TV5 and One Sports, called international volleyball for Volleyball World, and written and presented automotive stories for AutoIndustriya.com and Manila Bulletin. Before that, radio was a big part of his career. Nearly 25 years of it, as a presenter, program director and production lead. That range shows up in the way he works. Whether he’s writing, editing or speaking live on air, Eric has a knack for making technical or fast-moving subjects easier to understand without stripping away the detail that makes them interesting. Subscribe to the HotCars newsletter to never miss an update For years, the luxury sedan shorthand was easy. Buy German if you wanted steering feel and a chassis that seemed to enjoy an empty on-ramp as much as you did. Buy Japanese if you wanted something quieter, calmer, and less likely to make you send your service adviser a Facebook friend request. One sedan made that division much less tidy. It had a naturally aspirated V6, rear-wheel drive, adaptive dampers, 19-inch performance tires, larger brakes, quick steering, and even available rear-wheel steering. Contemporary testing showed the hardware wasn't there just to fill a brochure. The F Sport's case was made underneath the body. Lexus fitted firmer springs, thicker anti-roll bars, revised bushings, adaptive dampers, and quicker variable-ratio steering. Rear-drive cars also got staggered 19-inch performance tires, which gave the GS considerably more cornering intent than the typical Japanese executive sedan of the period. The available rear-steering system added another layer. Lexus said the system could turn the rear wheels opposite the fronts at lower speeds and, in certain conditions above 50 mph, in the same direction to improve agility and stability. On the road, the idea was simple: make a fairly large sedan feel less reluctant to turn and more settled once the speed came up. Car and Driver found out just how much of that hardware translated to the pavement. The rear-drive performance model reached 60 mph in 5.5 seconds, pulled 0.89 g on the skidpad, and stopped from 70 mph in 160 feet, while running within a tenth of a second of a contemporary BMW 535i to 60 mph. Those results came from Car and Driver's instrumented test of the fourth-generation car. The steering wasn't perfect. And “BMW handling” certainly doesn't mean the GS beat BMW at its own game. Car and Driver still described the steering feel as synthetic even while praising the car's grip, brakes, and high handling limits. BMW was simply a credible benchmark for this sedan, which was already a pretty surprising place for this particular Japanese luxury brand to find itself. The mystery sedan is the fourth-generation Lexus GS 350 F Sport, launched for the 2013 model year. And no, this wasn't an IS F with a quieter exhaust or a regular GS wearing an angry body kit. It was Lexus's midsize luxury sedan with enough real chassis work to truly deserve the F Sport badge. At launch, the GS 350 used a 3.5-liter naturally aspirated V6 producing 306 horsepower and 277 lb-ft of torque. Rear-wheel drive and all-wheel drive were both available, while the 2013 rear-drive version used a six-speed automatic with paddle shifters, quicker shifts, and throttle blips on downshifts. The F Sport badge went considerably deeper than wheels and trim. It brought F Sport-tuned Adaptive Variable Suspension, firmer springs, thicker anti-roll bars, revised bushings, 19-inch wheels, and larger front brakes on rear-drive cars, while Sport S+ sharpened the adaptive suspension, steering, and powertrain settings. Edmunds found that the changes worked, praising quick turn-in, rapid transitions, good balance, and plenty of adjustability during its track testing. Yet it still had to be a GS. Testers found the F Sport comfortable enough to work as a proper executive sedan despite the sharper chassis. Edmunds' track test and Car and Driver's review both landed on roughly the same point: the car got much sharper without turning every expansion joint into a personal attack. A used sports sedan can be cheap to buy and spectacularly expensive to keep. The Lexus badge suddenly becomes much more relevant once the car is a decade old. Strong handling numbers don't mean much if the car spends every other weekend sitting on top of a car lift. The GS 350 F Sport's appeal is that its reputation doesn't begin and end with what it can do on the track. J.D. Power gives the 2013 Lexus GS 350 an 89/100 Quality & Reliability score and lists the model as a Dependability Award winner. Consumer Reports also rates some later fourth-generation GS models well for reliability. It says the 2014 GS is more reliable than most cars from that year, while the 2015 GS is much more reliable than its peers. Put together, those ratings give the GS's reliability reputation more than just a Lexus badge to lean on. The 2013 car complicates the story a little. Consumer Reports currently rates it about average for reliability compared with other cars from the same model year, so calling every fourth-generation GS "bulletproof" would be doing the car no favors. Its 2013 GS reliability page is a good reminder that Lexus reliability doesn't repeal the laws of aging, maintenance, or previous-owner creativity. None of these cars are young anymore, and F Sport versions have more chassis hardware to inspect than a basic luxury sedan. A pre-purchase inspection should cover the service history, suspension and steering, adaptive damping, electronics, infotainment, wheels and tires, and any evidence of leaks or neglected maintenance. A GS 350 F Sport can still break, especially after more than a decade on the road. What makes it appealing is that its reliability record makes the usual old-luxury-car gamble look a little less frightening. The GS 350 F Sport feels more unusual now than it did in 2013. Back then, a naturally aspirated V6, rear-wheel drive, a conventional automatic, and adaptive suspension weren't especially exotic ingredients in a luxury sedan. Today, that combination is getting hard to find. The GS competed with cars such as the BMW 5 Series, Mercedes-Benz E-Class, Audi A6, Cadillac CTS, Infiniti M/Q70, and Acura RL/RLX. Some of those nameplates have disappeared, others have changed direction, and the segment itself has been squeezed by crossovers, electrification, downsized turbo engines, and increasingly software-heavy luxury cars. Against today's luxury market, the old GS suddenly has more character than its 2013 spec sheet suggested. Depreciation strengthens the case, although current asking prices should always be checked close to publication because mileage, condition, drivetrain, and model year move the numbers around substantially. A comparable BMW may still give a purist more steering feel or a broader engine menu, while a standard Lexus might suit someone who has never once wondered what a skidpad number means. The GS 350 F Sport sits between those two ideas, which is exactly why it works. Lexus eventually ended GS production in 2020 after four generations, leaving this particular combination without a direct successor. That makes the fourth-generation F Sport feel more significant now than when it was simply another new luxury sedan competing for showroom space. Does it handle exactly like a BMW 5 Series? No. The better question is how many used luxury sedans can still give you this much grip, comfort, naturally aspirated power, and Lexus durability in the same car. We want to hear from you. title: Karol G’s ‘Bby Wow’ Briefly Dethrones a Historic No. 1 Hit on Apple Music - Remezcla
content: VATICAN CITY, VATICAN - SEPTEMBER 13: Karol G attends the "Grace For The World" event at St. Peter's Square on September 13, 2025 in Vatican City, Vatican. (Photo by Daniele Venturelli/Getty Images for Grace For The World) Karol G has pulled off a chart feat many thought unlikely: ending Ella Langley’s reign at No. 1. Over Labor Day weekend, the Colombian singer knocked “Choosin’ Texas” from the top of the U.S. Apple Music all-genre songs chart. Her single “BbY WOW,” a collaboration with Spanish artists Judeline and Rusowsky, rose to No. 1, dethroning Langley’s country-pop smash after one of the longest runs in chart history. “Choosin’ Texas” has spent much of 2026 looking like a permanent fixture at the top. Langley’s song has dominated across virtually every major measure of U.S. music consumption. On the Billboard Hot 100, “Choosin’ Texas” reached its 20th week at No. 1 on the chart dated Sept. 5, making it the longest-running non-holiday song in the history of the 68-year-old chart. Only Mariah Carey’s “All I Want for Christmas Is You,” with 22 weeks, has spent more time at No. 1. The song has also logged historic runs on multiple charts while becoming one of the year’s defining crossover country hits. By late August, it had already spent 16 weeks at No. 1 on Digital Song Sales and 17 weeks atop Streaming Songs. That makes Karol G’s Apple Music upset more than just another chart shuffle. It’s significant because listeners chose a different rhythm to close out the summer-long weekend. Beyond the U.S. Apple Music charts, “BbY WOW” has also surged internationally, reaching No. 1 on Apple Music’s global chart and Spotify’s Global Top 50, while topping Billboard’s Hot Latin Songs chart. Still, the upset wasn’t permanent. As of today (Tuesday, Sept. 8), “BbY WOW” has slipped to No. 2. Even so, the significance is clear: “BbY WOW” did what most songs in 2026 haven’t managed so far—and that’s a victory worth recognizing and celebrating. The move came during a session in which megacap technology names also slipped, even as select industrial and housing-linked names advanced, underscoring how unevenly the hot labor-market data rippled through equity markets. For Goldman Sachs, long regarded as a bellwether for Wall Street's guidance, underwriting, and trading businesses, the pullback arrived even as the firm's capital-markets franchise continued generating headlines, from a marquee stabilization mandate tied to a closely watched technology listing to a broader push into digital-asset settlement alongside a roster of global banking peers. The combination of a challenging rate backdrop and an active dealmaking calendar leaves Goldman Sachs at the center of conversations about how diversified financial institutions balance near-term market volatility against longer-running franchise momentum. The session's driver was a jobs report that came in firmer than most market watchers had penciled in, reviving talk that the Federal Reserve could tighten its stance further rather than ease it, a scenario that had seemed increasingly unlikely earlier in the year. Bond markets moved quickly, with yields on government debt climbing as traders repriced the odds of another rate hike, a shift that tends to pressure bank shares in the near term even when it eventually supports the net interest margins those same banks earn on loans and securities. Goldman Sachs, with a business mix skewed more toward capital-markets activity, wealth management, and trading than toward traditional deposit-taking, tends to react to rate-path shifts differently than more retail-focused peers. Higher yields can complicate fixed-rate trading conditions in the short run, yet a steeper rate path over time often widens the spread banks earn on client balances, a dynamic that market participants continue to weigh as they gauge how the latest data shift affects diversified banks headed into the back half of the year. Goldman Sachs operates as one of the most recognized global banks anchored in capital-markets guidance, underwriting, trading, and asset and wealth management, with a franchise built over generations of relationships with corporations, institutions, and governments worldwide. The firm's guidance arm regularly ranks among the busiest in arranging mergers, acquisitions, and public offerings, while its trading operations span equities, fixed-rate instruments, currencies, and commodities. Beyond the marquee dealmaking business, Goldman Sachs has spent recent years broadening its asset and wealth management arm, aiming to build steadier, fee-based revenue streams that complement the inherently uneven cadence of guidance and underwriting work. That diversification push has reshaped how market participants view the firm, shifting the narrative from a pure trading and guidance shop toward a broader diversified financial institution with multiple engines of growth. Among the more closely watched storylines tied to Goldman Sachs recently is its reported role in a blockbuster technology listing, where the bank is said to be lined up for a stabilization mandate overseeing early trading once shares begin changing hands. Such mandates, while not guaranteed until formally finalized, tend to reinforce a bank's standing among the small handful of institutions capable of managing the most complex, highly anticipated public offerings. Separately, Goldman Sachs is among more than a dozen major global banks organizing a joint venture aimed at issuing a dollar-linked digital settlement instrument, a push that would extend the firm's footprint into digital-asset infrastructure alongside traditional guidance and trading lines. The initiative, still in its early planning stages, reflects how established banks are moving to shape emerging payment rails rather than cede that ground to newer entrants. Diversified banks and capital-markets firms sit within the broader Financial Stocks category, a group that spans commercial lenders, regional banks, insurers, and Wall Street guidance and trading houses alike. Within that category, Goldman Sachs stands out for its comparatively light reliance on traditional deposit-taking and lending, leaning instead on fee-based guidance work, trading activity, and a growing wealth management arm that together shape how the firm performs across different phases of the rate cycle. That positioning matters especially in periods like the current one, when a shifting rate path creates uneven effects across the category. Retail-heavy banks often feel the impact of rate moves through deposit costs and loan demand, while capital-markets-heavy firms such as Goldman Sachs tend to feel it through trading volumes, deal volumes, and the broader appetite for public offerings and mergers. The jobs-data-driven pullback in financial shares was not confined to Goldman Sachs. Peers spanning both diversified Wall Street firms and larger regional lenders eased in sympathy, reflecting how closely correlated the group remains despite differing business mixes. Meanwhile, dealmaking activity across the industry has shown signs of a broader pickup, with several large technology and healthcare transactions moving through various stages of preparation. The reported technology listing preparation, which is said to involve multiple major banks beyond Goldman Sachs, illustrates how concentrated the largest, most closely watched mandates remain among a small handful of firms with the scale and relationships to manage transactions of that size. Such mandates carry meaningful reputational weight even when the direct near-term financial contribution is modest relative to the overall firm. Treasury yields moved higher across the curve as traders absorbed the jobs data, a shift that touches nearly every corner of financial markets, from mortgage pricing to corporate borrowing costs to the discount rates used to value long-duration equities. For banks broadly, a steeper and higher yield curve is often viewed constructively over time, even though the immediate market reaction skewed negative for financial shares. The broader S&P 500 eased alongside financial shares as market participants weighed the jobs data against ongoing questions about the pace of the Federal Reserve's next moves. Megacap technology names led losses in the broader tape, while select industrial and housing-linked names advanced, a divergence that underscores how unevenly the labor-market surprise rippled through different corners of the market. Beyond the day's price action, several longer-running trends continue to shape how diversified banks like Goldman Sachs are viewed. Digital-asset infrastructure, including the joint stablecoin venture the firm has joined alongside more than a dozen peers, represents one such trend, as banks race to build compliant, bank-grade payment rails before newer entrants can capture that ground. Another trend involves the steady push toward fee-based, less capital-intensive revenue streams, a shift that has pushed Goldman Sachs and similar firms to expand wealth and asset management arms even as guidance and trading remain the more recognized parts of the business. That diversification effort aims to smooth out the historically uneven, deal-cycle-dependent nature of Wall Street earnings. Goldman Sachs continues to position itself as a diversified financial institution rather than a pure trading and guidance shop, emphasizing the steadier fee streams generated by its wealth and asset management arm alongside the more headline-grabbing guidance and underwriting business. That positioning has become a recurring theme in how the firm frames its own narrative to market participants and the broader public. The firm's scale across guidance, underwriting, trading, and wealth management gives it exposure to multiple parts of the economic cycle simultaneously, a structure that can cushion swings in any single business line. That said, the diversified structure does not eliminate sensitivity to broad market conditions, as the day's pullback across financial shares demonstrated. Operationally, Goldman Sachs has continued emphasizing efficiency alongside growth, a balance that has become increasingly common across large Wall Street institutions as they weigh the costs of maintaining sprawling trading and guidance operations against the fee revenue those businesses generate. Technology spending, including efforts tied to digital-asset infrastructure and settlement rails, forms part of that broader efficiency push. The firm's wealth management arm, in particular, has become an area of sustained operational focus, as Goldman Sachs works to expand its base of high-net-worth and institutional relationships in a bid to build steadier, recurring fee revenue that complements the inherently cyclical nature of guidance and trading work. Diversified banks including Goldman Sachs continue to navigate a list of familiar exposures, from shifting Federal Reserve rate expectations to regulatory scrutiny to competitive pressure from both traditional peers and newer, technology-driven entrants. The latest jobs data adds a fresh layer of uncertainty to that list, as market participants reassess how a firmer labor market and higher yields might reshape the rate path over coming quarters. Regulatory factors also remain a constant backdrop for firms of Goldman Sachs's size and systemic footprint, with capital and liquidity requirements shaping how much flexibility the firm has to expand its balance sheet, return capital to stockholders, or pursue new lines of business such as digital-asset settlement. Goldman Sachs competes across multiple fronts simultaneously, facing rival Wall Street firms in guidance and underwriting, larger universal banks in trading and financing, and a growing field of independent wealth managers in the fee-based guidance space. That multi-front competitive landscape has pushed the firm to defend its standing in traditional strongholds while also building out newer, faster-growing business lines. The reported competition among major banks for top roles in the largest technology listings highlights how concentrated the most prestigious mandates remain among a handful of firms with the scale, relationships, and balance-sheet capacity to manage transactions of that size and complexity. Goldman Sachs maintains relationships spanning multinational corporations, sovereign entities, pension funds, and family offices across nearly every major economy, a global reach that few rivals can match. That breadth of relationships underpins the firm's ability to win mandates on the largest, most complex cross-border transactions, from public offerings to mergers spanning multiple jurisdictions. The firm's global footprint also means its results are sensitive to conditions well beyond domestic markets, including shifts in European and Asian dealmaking activity, currency swings, and regional regulatory developments, all of which factor into how market participants read the firm's quarterly performance. Goldman Sachs has long cultivated a reputation for recruiting and retaining top talent across trading, guidance, and wealth management, a competitive advantage the firm has worked to preserve even as compensation costs across Wall Street have climbed. Retaining senior dealmakers and traders remains an ongoing priority given how mobile talent can be within the industry. The firm's internal culture, often described as demanding and performance-driven, has also evolved gradually as Goldman Sachs works to broaden its base of steadier, fee-based businesses, a shift that has required blending the firm's traditional trading-floor intensity with the longer relationship-building approach more common in wealth management. Goldman Sachs has continued balancing capital return to stockholders through dividends and buyback activity against the need to maintain a sturdy balance sheet capable of supporting its trading and underwriting commitments. That balance has become an increasingly visible theme as market participants weigh how much flexibility the firm retains to fund new initiatives such as its digital-asset push. Maintaining a strong capital position also supports Goldman Sachs's ability to commit balance-sheet capacity to large underwriting and stabilization mandates, including the marquee technology listing role the firm is reported to be pursuing, since such mandates can require the bank to temporarily carry significant positions during the early trading period. Firm marks expansion in Washington state with ribbon-cutting ceremony, underscoring commitment to accelerating innovation and talent growth BELLEVUE, Wash. — September 8, 2026 — Goldman Sachs opened a new office today in Bellevue, Washington. The new location is the firm’s first dedicated space for engineers in the region and will accommodate more than 125 employees focused on artificial intelligence and cloud transformation. "We are in a period of rapid technological change, but we know our people are still this firm’s greatest asset. Hiring exceptional talent is central to how we adapt and grow," said David Solomon, chairman and CEO of Goldman Sachs. "The Pacific Northwest is home to many of the world’s top engineering schools and a deep pool of talent. Opening in Bellevue reflects our long-term commitment to attracting and developing technologists who want to work with the best and lead our industry through this next phase of change.” The new dedicated space gives Goldman Sachs a permanent footprint in one of the world's leading technology hubs and serves as a strategic presence to accelerate its firmwide AI and cloud transformation. The Bellevue, Wash. location provides access to a deep pool of engineering talent and a strong pipeline of graduates from leading universities, with expertise across cloud, AI and other emerging technologies. Goldman Sachs employs over 12,000 engineers, representing roughly one-quarter of the firm's global workforce, who play a critical role in developing the technologies that power its businesses. As technology and AI continue to transform the financial industry, the firm is at the forefront of equipping its engineers with advanced tools and platforms that help drive innovation, enhance productivity, and support clients. The Bellevue office expands Goldman Sachs' network of engineering hubs and complements the firm's presence since 2001 in downtown Seattle, housing employees across the firm’s Banking and Wealth Management businesses. This investment builds on the firm’s growth across the globe into locations including Dallas, Salt Lake City and Warsaw. The space features an open floor plan designed to foster collaboration, productivity and client service alongside wellness amenities, underscoring Goldman Sachs' commitment to providing a modern workplace experience that supports the well-being of its workforce. For employers considering an ESPP or thinking about restructuring, there are a number of regulatory, financial, and employee attraction and retention considerations. This article shares insights into how employers are responding to these pressures and the trends shaping the broader market. From an employer’s perspective, an employee stock purchase plan can be a strategic compensation benefit helping to directly align employees’ financial incentives with those of shareholders and the business. At the time of this report, a slight majority of employers offer an ESPP (52%).1 This decision often hinges on several considerations, including the strength of ownership culture across the workforce, how closely participation tracks market-standard rates, the expense borne by the company, and the cash flow available to employees. The data shows meaningful differences in ESPP adoption by industry. Employers in the Technology, Media, & Telecommunications industry had the highest rate of ESPP availability (68%), while employers in the Real Estate sector were least likely to offer ESPPs (17%). This range suggests that employers weigh factors such as industry-specific talent dynamics, capital structure, and compensation philosophy when deciding whether to offer the benefit. While employers use a number of metrics to define eligible participants for ESPPs, the most common is hours worked per week (36%). This can effectively remove part-time workers from eligibility pools. Tenure (32%) is also frequently used to limit participation eligibility. This can help encourage loyalty and support employee retention efforts. Exactly half of the plans reviewed apply a single metric to limit employee eligibility, indicating a preference for administrative simplicity. 32% of employers take a two-metric approach, while the remaining 18% utilize three limitations. Employers that offer ESPPs fall into one of three broad plan structures: Qualified Section 423 plans, nonqualified plans, and direct purchase plans. Qualified plans made up the largest share of plans reviewed (76%), while nonqualified (14%) and direct purchase plans (10%) appeared less frequently but may offer practical advantages for certain employer objectives. Qualified Section 423 plans (76%) may be particularly appealing to employers because of the potential tax benefits they can provide to eligible US employees. At the same time, they require strict regulatory compliance, shareholder approval, nondiscrimination rules, and the annual statutory purchase limit ($25,000 per participant). Nonqualified plans represent a smaller share of ESPPs reviewed (14%) but employers are looking at the design as an option that introduces more flexibility, eases administrative needs, and simplifies tax treatment.  Because these plans are not subject to the same Section 423 framework, they can support a broader range of eligibility rules and incentive structures. Eligibility rules, offering frequency, contribution limits, incentive structure, and pricing methodology can all affect how employees interact with the plan and how the employer manages cost, administration, and alignment with business priorities. title: Lunchbreak: ‘Where Every Team Stands’ as 2026 Kickoff Weekend Arrives - Minnesota Vikings
content:
The season begins tomorrow with a Super Bowl LX rematch. It continues Thursday in Australia between the Rams and the 49ers. And on Sunday, Minnesota hosts Green Bay in the 132nd Border Battle. It seems like an opportune time to assess where each team stands heading into the 2026 slate. That's exactly what Albert Breer did for Sports Illustrated this week. Here's what Breer wrote about the Purple in his check-in on the 32 clubs: The Vikings have had a reputation for being a great home for veteran quarterbacks that fell out of favor elsewhere, for one reason or another. It goes back to my childhood: Rich Gannon, Jim McMahon, Warren Moon, Randall Cunningham, Jeff George, Brett Favre and Kirk Cousins have all led Minnesota to the playoffs. Now they have Kyler Murray in to lead an offense with a ton of talent in the prime of their careers, with a veteran defense capable of maximizing Brian Flores's scheme. Note: Gannon was drafted by New England in 1987 but joined Minnesota that season. View photos of the Vikings 53-man roster as of Sep. 8, 2026. Breer noted that it's common for prognosticators to oversimplify things, insinuating that adding Murray to the mix is a solve-all for the franchise — "as if the quarterback is playing one-on-one hoops against the other team's quarterback," Breer wrote — but in this case there's some truth to it. Breer sees Murray being "that pivotal of a piece" and he highlighted Minnesota's confidence in the 29-year-old quarterback to bring dynamism to the offense on bootlegs, keepers and scramble drills. What else grabbed our attention in Breer's notebook? Well, thoughts on early season challengers. On the Packers, Breer conjectured that "this is already a good team. If its young guys can take the step from good to great, a la Seattle last year, then the Packers will be a true Super Bowl contender." As for Minnesota's opponents in Weeks 2 and 3 (Chicago and Tampa Bay) Breer focused on the respective quarterbacks: He cited his recent QB poll as proof that many people are expecting Caleb Williams to make a leap in his second season under Head Coach Ben Johnson; and Breer wondered whether there's still a deal to be done between the Buccaneers and Baker Mayfield, who is 27-24 in three seasons as Tampa Bay's starter and is second in the league with 95 passing TDs since 2023. Click here to read all of Breer's notes regarding the imminent campaign. Long before Vikings assistant defensive backs coach Chenzo Funari worked on Brian Flores' defense, he worked in a World War II-era garage in the Mojave Desert … on small rocket engines. Funari is the 32-year-old "secret weapon" who was profiled recently by The Athletic's Alec Lewis. The story of Funari's transition from science to the sidelines started in Southern California, in the middle of nowhere, before progressing into a volunteer coaching position at Youngstown State and landing him, eventually, in "a meaningful role on one of the most respected defensive staffs in the NFL." As a child, Funari fixated on two things: space and sports. He studied constellations. At the dinner table, he quizzed his parents on the solar system. (His sister) Taylor still doesn't know the answer to a question he'd constantly pose when he entered the living room: What is the average temperature on Mars? "It was like he was a walking encyclopedia," she said. The Cleveland native also adored the playing style of Hall of Fame quarterback Brett Favre. Maybe it was the fearlessness, possibly the flair. Funari practiced youth football with the gunslinger on his mind. His parents quickly recognized the sport was one of the few activities that gave his brain a break. Funari is entering his third season with the Vikings in 2026 and his second as a member of the coaching staff after joining the organization as a football quantitative methods associate. Although his background is unique, it serves him well. Players, including Harrison Smith, have gravitated toward his expertise. title: Goldman Stock Gains 38.6% in a Year: Buy Now or Wait for a Pullback? - The Globe and Mail
content: Shares of The Goldman Sachs GroupGS have gained 38.6% in the past year, outperforming the industry’s rise of 26.1%. Its peers, Morgan StanleyMS and JPMorgan’s JPM shares rose 46.2% and 22.6%, respectively, over the same time frame. With such strong momentum, investors may be wondering whether to buy the GS stock now or wait for a better entry point. To help answer this question, let us take a closer look at the key factors driving Goldman’s growth and assess whether the stock still has room to run. Merger and acquisition (M&A) advisory remains a key competitive strength for Goldman. Winning mandates on large transactions not only supports advisory revenues but can also generate opportunities across financing, underwriting and other client businesses. Recent league-table rankings highlight that strength. Goldman was the only adviser in South and Central America to exceed $10 billion in aggregate deal value during the first half of 2026, according to GlobalData. It also ranked first among North American M&A advisers by deal value, advising on $437.7 billion in transactions. The favorable M&A backdrop led Goldman to deliver strong results. GS’s IB fees rose 52% year over year in the first half of 2026, driven by higher advisory, equity underwriting and debt underwriting revenues amid improving capital markets activity. Management also sounded constructive about the operating environment following the second-quarter results. CEO David Solomon highlighted accelerating momentum across the company’s businesses and pointed to strong client demand for Goldman to advise on major strategic transactions. Management noted that the investment banking backlog reached its highest level in five years, including a record advisory backlog, supported by robust strategic M&A activity, AI-related capital formation and stronger financing demand. Goldman is undertaking an ambitious, firmwide artificial intelligence (AI) transformation aimed at boosting fee income, improving productivity and expanding long-term operating leverage. The initiative spans its core businesses, including trading, investment banking, asset management and internal operations, positioning AI as a central growth driver. In July, Yahoo Finance, citing Reuters, reported that Goldman Sachs Asset Management had launched AlphaAI, an artificial intelligence-focused investment platform. The initiative underscores the firm's conviction that AI will emerge as a significant driver of investment opportunities and returns across both public and private markets. Earlier, Goldman partnered with Anthropic on a $1.5-billion initiative designed to accelerate AI adoption across hundreds of portfolio companies. At the center of Goldman’s transformation are two major initiatives — One Goldman Sachs 3.0, or OneGS 3.0, and the GS AI Assistant program. OneGS 3.0 is a multi-year effort to integrate AI into the firm’s core operating model rather than treat it as a standalone technology. The program focuses on simplifying workflows, modernizing infrastructure and supporting scalable growth through shared platforms, standardized processes and higher-quality data. The GS AI Assistant is expected to further improve employee productivity by helping professionals analyze information, generate content and complete routine tasks more efficiently. As adoption expands, the platform could reduce manual workloads and allow employees to devote more time to client engagement, decision-making and higher-value activities. Management has expressed strong confidence in AI’s long-term potential. Although spending on AI, data and digital infrastructure may keep expenses elevated in the near term, the investments could generate meaningful productivity gains and help the firm move toward its medium-term efficiency ratio target of 60%. GS streamlining efforts have been underway for some time as it retreats from the underperforming consumer banking ventures. Under CEO David Solomon, GS has embarked on a deliberate transformation to exit non-core consumer banking and double down on the divisions wherein Goldman maintains a clear competitive advantage. In sync with its restructuring efforts, in August 2026, Goldman agreed to acquire NEOS Investments. The acquisition will add $30 billion in assets across NEOS's 19 options-based income ETFs to Goldman Sachs Asset Management's existing $40 billion in income and outcome-oriented options-based ETF solutions. Once complete, the deal will make Goldman Sachs Asset Management the eighth-largest active ETF provider. In April 2026, GS acquired Innovator Capital Management, expanding its active ETF capabilities as part of a broader strategy to build durable revenue streams through diversified asset and wealth management offerings.  In the same month, Goldman completed the divestiture of its Polish asset management business, Goldman Sachs TFI, to ING Bank Slaski, further streamlining its asset management operations. In the third quarter of 2025, the company transitioned the General Motors credit card program. These moves demonstrate a well-thought-out exit, allowing the company to reallocate capital and attention toward higher-margin, more scalable businesses like Global Banking and Markets, and the asset and wealth management divisions. Goldman maintains a fortress balance sheet, with the Tier 1 capital ratios well above regulatory requirements. This financial strength allows it to return capital to its shareholders aggressively through buybacks and a healthy dividend yield. As of June 30, 2026, cash and cash equivalents were $187 billion, while deposits totaled $558 billion. Total unsecured debt (comprising long-term and short-term borrowings) was $438 billion, of which only $90 billion was near-term borrowings. Following the Federal Reserve’s 2026 stress test, the company increased its quarterly common stock dividend by 11% to $5 per share. The company also has a share repurchase plan in place. title: Vikings & Legends Global Announce U.S. Bank Stadium Enhancements for 2026 - Minnesota Vikings
content:
EAGAN, Minn. — The Minnesota Vikings and Legends Global are introducing a series of technology enhancements for the 2026 season at U.S. Bank Stadium. The changes, which include innovative entry procedures and an upgraded retail experience, are designed to make every visit, from arrival through departure, seamless for fans. Descriptions and links to video tutorials for each stadium enhancement are below. Open the Gates: Faster, Frictionless Security Screening U.S. Bank Stadium has enhanced the fan arrival experience with the installation of new OpenGate security screening technology at every entry point. The advanced contactless system allows guests to move through security screening without removing items from their pockets or having approved bags physically inspected, helping create a faster and more convenient entry process while enhancing stadium security. The clear bag policy that limits the size of bags allowed in the venue remains in effect. After trialing the technology in limited fashion during the 2025 season, the Vikings are expanding Vikings Express Pass, a voluntary touchless entry program powered by biometric authentication technology. The optional program allows enrolled guests to enter through designated lanes and eliminates the need to scan individual tickets or present a mobile device at the gate. Fans simply walk through the entry lane while their full allotment of tickets are automatically validated, reducing wait times and creating a seamless and efficient arrival experience when paired with the stadium's touchless security screening. Seven touchless entry lanes are available at five gate locations across the stadium, including the Legacy Gate, CFMOTO Gate, Ticketmaster Gate, Ecolab Gate and Upper 3M Gate. Participation is completely voluntary, and traditional ticket-scanning options remain available for all guests. Interested fans can sign up in advance here. Fans shopping at the Vikings Locker Room Store on the main concourse will enjoy a faster and more convenient checkout experience with the introduction of RFID self-checkout technology. The new system allows guests to simply place selected merchandise into a checkout station, where RFID technology instantly identifies all items at once and displays the purchase total for payment. The process eliminates the need to scan items individually, helping reduce lines and create a seamless shopping experience. In 2026, the Minnesota Vikings welcomed CFMOTO and TCL as new partners and expanded the team's longstanding relationship with 3M. As part of these new and expanded partnerships, several key locations throughout U.S. Bank Stadium have been updated. Fans entering the stadium will now find the CFMOTO Gate, Lower 3M Gate and Upper 3M Gate, while premium seating sections V1-V5 are now part of the TCL Club. Additional enhancements throughout the stadium include the introduction of the Miller Lite Bar on the main concourse and an expanded partnership with Factory Motor Parts, which now serves as the entitlement sponsor of the stadium parking garage. Guests are encouraged to review stadium maps, mobile tickets and Know Before You Go communications prior to arrival to ensure a smooth gameday experience. title: BMW Motorrad launches new F 450 GS in South Korea, starting at W12.5m - 헤럴드경제
content: BMW Motorrad, the motorcycle division of BMW, announced Tuesday it is launching the BMW New F 450 GS premium adventure motorcycle in South Korea. The BMW New F 450 GS is an entirely new model designed to bring the GS series' signature on- and off-road riding experience to a wider range of riders through a lighter frame and more accessible handling. In terms of design, the front features full LED headlights with an X-shaped daytime running light, combined with a sharply forward-swept nose and dynamic body lines that give the motorcycle an unmistakably bold GS family look. The bodywork incorporates GS-defining design elements throughout, including the signature "beak," "tooth" and distinctive flyline. The sleek silhouette running from the fuel tank through the seat to the rear emphasizes a light, dynamic character, while the center section of the 14-liter fuel tank is slimmed down to allow riders to brace the bike securely with their knees whether seated or standing. Built on a curb weight of 178 kilograms and an entirely new chassis, the BMW New F 450 GS delivers agile yet stable riding performance. Both front and rear suspension offer 180 millimeters of travel, covering a wide range of on- and off-road conditions. The front uses a 43mm inverted telescopic fork, while the rear employs an aluminum double swingarm with a central spring strut. Lightweight cast aluminum wheels — 19 inches at the front and 17 inches at the rear — paired with dual-sport tires round out the setup for stable riding across varied surfaces. The BMW New F 450 GS is powered by a 420cc parallel-twin engine producing 48 hp and a maximum torque of 4.4 kg·m. The powertrain was developed from the outset specifically for the F 450 GS, engineered to deliver strong performance and sharp responsiveness despite its compact, lightweight construction. A new six-speed gearbox comes standard across all trims, along with Shift Assistant Pro, which enables quick upshifts and downshifts without operating the clutch lever in most riding situations. The GS Trophy trim of the BMW New F 450 GS comes standard with the new Easy Ride Clutch (ERC), a system that uses a precision centrifugal mechanism to automatically engage and disengage the clutch based on engine speed. The BMW New F 450 GS also offers four riding modes to handle a variety of surfaces and conditions: Rain, Road, Enduro and Enduro Pro. Safety electronics include ABS Pro for stable braking through corners, Dynamic Traction Control (DTC) to suppress rear-wheel slip, Dynamic Brake Control (DBC) to prevent unintended throttle input during hard braking, and engine drag torque control to reduce rear-wheel slide during deceleration. The cockpit features a 6.5-inch TFT color display with sharp graphics and excellent visibility. Riders can intuitively check key riding data — including speed, engine rpm, DTC status, braking force and lean angle — and easily select the appropriate riding mode for any environment. The BMW New F 450 GS goes on sale in South Korea in two trims: Exclusive and GS Trophy, priced at 12.5 million won ($9,310) and 13.5 million won, respectively. Meanwhile, BMW Motorrad recently launched the BMW Motorrad Vantage app, an integrated lifestyle platform for motorcycle customers. BMW Vantage, first introduced in 2020 as the automotive industry's first lifestyle platform, offers a wide range of services spanning mobility, travel, culture and education, built around "Vantage Coin," a membership points currency exclusive to customers.
